raw_comment:
What do you notice?:
    I noticed that girls tend to get better grades than boys do, fixing the norm that they take the lead in many criteria. They take the leading role in school, as well as participating; therefore making them the teachers “favorites”. It’s not that teachers may favor the girls because of their gender, but it is because of participation. Teachers enjoy when a student is actively engaging in class, making teaching an overly positive environment and workspace for teachers. 
    
    What do you wonder?:
    I wonder what is stopping boys from participating in the classroom. This can tie in with the fact that our current generation has declined in social norms. They feel as if it is “weird” or awkward to raise their hands or speak up in classrooms. If there was more encouragement in conversing with their teachers, I feel there would be a much higher percentage in boys, or even both in equal terms. 
    
    Relation to me:
    This graph relates to my community because of how it correlates to educational differences between girls and boys. I notice in classrooms, teachers are more attracted to the loud and social students, finding joy in having conversation with them. 
    
    Headline:
    Why do girls do better in school?

raw_comment:
Girls consistently earn better grades than they’re seen as teacher’s favorites, suggesting that the rise in female teachers doesn’t disadvantage boys — they get equal attention. The issue may instead be that boys pay less attention to female teachers due to social norms about interacting with women.
    
    I wonder if girls have always been stronger academically but were once held back by limited access or encouragement. And if girls now outperform boys in school, why doesn’t that lead to greater leadership or success after graduation?
    
    Anthropologically, this shift could reduce coupling: high-achieving women may avoid partnering with men who can’t match their ambitions or still expect traditional domestic roles — as seen in a number of Asian countries. In a more macro scale there's a national safety issue at hand as well. 
    
    So what did once motivate boys? That's the question. Was it teacher support, peer competition, social expectations, or the clear link between academic success and future prosperity — a link that feels weaker today? Could it be all of the above which boys now satisfy through playing video games? Maybe we need a similar survey of 60, 70, and 80 year-olds to compare, and/or a survey of single gendered schools to see if there's any difference there. 
    
    Title: Girls do better in school. So what?

raw_comment:
Who will become more successful? Boys or Girls?
    
    My first interpretation of this graph was the significant difference in percent of which male and female bodies are shown in academic excellence, teacher favorites, and leadership.In the graph, females have seem to dominate in all 3 fields. The age group strikes a question of whether the lower ages would deem themselves "better", so they would just pick their own gender. Could the school/place this information was collected be an all female area, such as an all girls k-12 school, or a salon. This relates to my community in such a way that if the NYT attempted to collect information in a child development class, with majority female bodies, the graph could be even more biased. If NYT tried to collect the same information in a male dominated class, such as woodwork, the information on the graph would be different.

    I do have a lot of questions in regards to this, mainly about the demographic of the students who answered. What type of school do they go to? What gender were the students who answered?     All in all, the graph tells us that teens mostly believe the  spread of acceleration in these categories in school is relatively even, but when it comes down to giving a specific answer, they typically answer "girls".

raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of the graph categories are a combination of both genders, however, when singled out girls got a higher percentage than boys did in each category, showing how their skills often dominated over the male students on average.
    
    This makes me wonder... Why do boys have such a lower percentage than girls do in the categories? What could be altered/changed within school in order to increase the boys percentage? What categories do you think they could add to this graph in order to get a higher male percentage? If we added a category of sport participation or creativity would the percentage of male students increase?
    
    I've noticed within my own personal school experience that male students tend to be more immature on average than female students due to their later developments and differences in our brains and physical development. Women often tend to show more traits of leadership, communication, and respect than male students on average. 
    
    The frontal cortex of women often matures faster than men's, this part of the brain focuses on empathy, appropriate social behaviors, decision-making, impulse control, memory, planning, and adapting to new situations.
    
    "The Gender Clash Of Skills" or "The Gender Dominance Within A School Environment", showing differences from male students' academic skills in certain categories in comparison to female students', showing the dominance difference between the two through compare and contrast.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
    Most U.S. teens think girls generally do better in school. 42% percent of survey participants said girls get better grades, whereas only 3% said boys do. More students also said girls speak up and ask more questions (34%) and hold more leadership roles (27%). Many teens see both genders to be excelling equally, as the equal section was still the largest in every category.
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder about whether they conducted the survey's results would change when comparing the different types of schools, like catholic, private, or public, and different regions, since political leaning of the region can impact their opinion. Maybe even grade levels impact this as well due to exposure to more people and maturity levels.
    
    3. How does this relate to you and your community?
    I’ve noticed that girls are more active in class and also take more leadership roles in clubs. I think that boys sometimes hesitate to speak up in class. Looking at the graph, its a reminder to build a community that allows participation in class and leadership roles without gender playing a role, since education is for everyone and shouldn't be 'cool' for only 1 gender to be participating. An equal encouragement needs to start from homes to promote academic equality.
    
    4. Catchy headline:
    “Equality or Female Supremacy? What's the students' take on academic excellence”

raw_comment:
1. I notice that for each question asked, the highest percentage of those surveyed thought that both genders excelled equally, the second-highest percentage refers to those who thought girls excel more, and the least percentage thought boys excel more. For example, 48% thought boys and girls speak up equal amounts in school, 34% thought girls speak up more, and 18% thought boys speak up more. This order of percentages from greatest to least is consistent throughout the four categories. 
    2. I wonder how the results would be different if this survey was conducted in the past. Specifically, I’m curious when exactly the shift was from boys dominating the classroom (a safe assumption considering males had historically better access to education) to the perception of girls excelling more in schools, and how the survey data could change alongside the socioeconomic status of women. 
    3. As a female student in high school, it’s interesting and somewhat encouraging that the academic efforts of teenage girls like myself aren’t going unnoticed. Additionally, data such as these could raise questions about achievement recognition in the community. For example, schools might be curious about whether girls do excel more in these categories or if they’re just perceived as more studious and why that might be. Answering these questions could influence how the community acknowledges academic achievement.
    4. Inside the Teenage Mind: Are Girls Really Better at School?

    Signing off – Jamie Perrett from Salem, Utah, who thinks that both male and female students are amazing! and Chris Luzniak from Columbus, Ohio, who agrees and loved reading all the responses!

raw_comment: In this graph, I notice that most of the time, boys and girls rank about equal in every category. When not equal, girls take the majority over boys. I notice girls have better grades and speak up more. I wonder if this lead of girls is because of the constant underestimation of girls in society. Has the perception of girls being less than or weaker pushed them to outperform others in school? Or is it a lack of effort being put in by boys nowadays? If so, why have they lost interest or drive? 1. I notice that for every category, most kids said that boys and girls were both about equal. Also, in every category, Girls were always the next option; therefore, boys were always last. raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
    Most U.S. teens think girls generally do better in school. Forty-two percent of participants said girls get better grades, while only 3% said boys do. More students also said girls speak up and ask questions more (34%) and hold more leadership roles (27%). Many teens see strengths in both genders, as the equal section was still the largest in every category 
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder about whether they conducted their research and if there's an intersection to the results, like if results would change when comparing the different types of schools, like catholic or public, and different regions, maybe even if grade levels impact this as well. 
    
    3. How does this relate to you and your community?
    At my school, I’ve noticed that girls are often more active in class and also take more leadership roles in clubs. I think that boys sometimes hold back in class and usually take leadership roles in sports rather than clubs. Looking at the graph its seemingly a reminder to build a community that allows participation in class and leadership roles without gender playing a role.
    
    4. Catchy headline:
    “Girls Lead the Class: Teens Say Female Students Excel Beyond Grades”

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
    In the graph I notice that in all of the categories the dominating consensus is that both are about equal in all of the categories. 3 out of 4 of the categories have over a 50% majority voting that both are equal. Even in the 4th category, Speak up more,  where the division stating both are equal does not have a 50% majority over the other divisions; it still has the highest percentage in the whole category. When I looked beyond the both are equal divisions I noticed that girls are determined to be better than boys in all the categories; including better grades (42% to 3%), more leader roles (27% to 16%), teacher favorites (16% to 6%), and speak up more (34% to 18%).
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder two things. The first thing I wonder is that if this survey was of teenage students worldwide, would we get a different consensus or would it remain about the same? Another thing I wonder is if there were only two response options, boys and girls, would girls still beat boys in all the categories?
    
    3. How does this relate to you and your community?
    This impacts me and my community because my community could share similar beliefs to the people who took this survey, since we are also teenagers in the U.S. It could also reflect how students view their own capabilities in the academic world.
     
    4. Create a catchy headline.
    We Say It’s Equal But is it Really? What Teens Reveal About the Role of Gender Within Schools

raw_comment:
1. Girls are perceived as having better grades than boys, with only 3% of boys estimated to have better
    grades. Although 55% said that both boys are girls are about equal. Leadership, on the other hand, is
    more mixed and not as much influenced by the gender of the student.
    2. I wonder how many students were actually surveyed to create this chart and present these findings.
    3. I never thought that there could be a gender bias in schools and educational purposes, which could
    shape the way that people think. Seeing that around 42% of people think girls have better grades makes
    me wonder if there are different expectations for students based on their gender.
    4. Battle of Gender Perceptions in Schools.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that when disregarding the “both about equal” portion, girls were mostly said to excel in those categories more than boys, except for the “speak up more” category, where results were more equal. Around 50% of respondents said boys and girls were about equal in all categories except “teacher favorites,” which could be explained by differing personalities in teachers. The survey was conducted between September 18 and October 10, which is early in the school year when teachers and students are still getting comfortable with each other. This could explain why almost half of the respondents in each topic said boys and girls were about equal.
    
    2. I wonder if the opinions of those who didn’t answer differed from those who did and if the results are biased. I also wonder if they missed respondents from certain parts of the country whose responses could have been different. Could there be a pattern based on school location and how U.S. teenagers ages 13 to 17 compare in each category?
    
    3. This impacts me and my community because if we acknowledge the perceived gender bias in this study, we can work to ensure opportunities remain equal by educating others. I think our school would show similar results: girls seem more focused on grades, leadership feels about equal, teacher favorites depend on personality, and both genders seem equally likely to speak up.
    
    4. Gender and success at school through the eyes of a teenager.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? 
    
    In all sections, most respondents viewed boys and girls as equally capable. However, when compared directly, the data suggest that girls were perceived to excel in every area, being teacher favorites (16% vs. 6%), earning better grades (42% vs. 3%), speaking up more in class (34% vs. 18%), and even taking on more leadership roles (27% vs. 16%).
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    
    Since the survey did not include homeschooled students, I wonder how their answers might change the results. I also wonder whether a larger sample size would change our results.
    
    3. How does this relate to you and your community?
    
    This relates to me and my community because these perceptions could influence gender expectations and how students view their own abilities in school.
    
    4. Catchy Title:
    
    Girls vs. Boys: Who Excels in School?

raw_comment:
1. Teenagers responded that both genders are about equal for at least 50% in every category. The one exception is the “Speak up more” category, where more teens chose a specific gender rather than claiming that both are equal. Another pattern is that, in all of the categories, girls are the second most chosen response, whereas boys are third.
    
    2. Would including homeschooled students strengthen these patterns or introduce new ones? Did the survey include only co-ed schools, or were students from all boys/girls schools questioned as well? If they were, how would their opinions differ? Would breaking these categories down into more specific ones (such as better grades in specific classes) return the same general results?
    
    3. This survey relates to my community as the results reflect what I’ve observed throughout high school. As a senior, I’ve already been in many classes with different groups of students, and I’ve seen both girls and boys fall into each of these categories in all of these classes. As a result, I believe that gender is rarely the variable that determines if someone fits into any of these categories. Furthermore, these results mirror my out-of-class experiences. Whether it’s with my friends, at a club, or in sports, I’ve noticed that categories such as leadership and participation are generally not determined by gender.
    
    4. Who Excels in School? What Teens Actually Think About Boys vs. Girls

For example, though 55% of those surveyed said that both girls and boys received better grades, 42% of the respondents said that girls were more likely to receive better grades while 3% of them vouched for the boys. This pattern continues in the remaining categories with 27% of the respondents claiming that girls had more leadership roles while 16% of the respondents believed that boys excelled here. Additionally, 34% of the respondents said that girls were more likely to speak up while 18% of them thought boys spoke up more. By the majority of the respondents that didn’t pick both about equal, boys were seen as less excelling than girls in these four categories but not overwhelmingly so. 
    2. I also wonder if the data would look different (and how) if other age groups and homeschooled students were surveyed. Lastly, I wonder if there was any bias in how the teenagers answered the survey and what this bias could’ve been. 
    3. Though the majority of respondents claimed that they believed girls and boys both equally excelled in these categories, I think that the fact that the other half of the respondents believed that girls were more excelling than boys could influence how boys and girls view their own abilities and opportunities in academics and leadership.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    
    I notice that for all of the categories, most of the teens surveyed thought that excellence was even for boys and girls. However, for the people who didn't think it was even, the teenagers thought that it was more girls who were doing better. For most of the categories, in general, the teenagers didn't think that boys were the ones who excelled in grades, leadership, teacher's favorites, and speaking up.
    
    What do you wonder?
    
    I wonder why so many people thought that girls excel more than boys do, specifically in better grades and speaking up more. What influenced the teenagers to make the choice they made? Were an even number of boys and girls surveyed? I wonder who these kids were and where they went to school, because this all would affect the data. 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community? 
    
    In my school, I definitely believe that girls do a lot more leadership, speaking up, and engagement within classes, which ultimately causes teachers to like them more. I also think that girls tend to try harder in school, which results in getting better grades. Overall, I think the graph is very similar to how I believe our school would show if we were surveyed. However, I think more teenagers would respond that girls did better than responding that it was even between the two. 
    
    Create a catchy headline. 
    
    Teens say that girls outshine boys in academic excellence.

raw_comment:
1.I notice that on all of the polls, at least 50% of the teens surveyed stated that both boys and girls are equal in
    each category. I also noticed that, on average, those surveyed say that girls get better grades, have more lead
    roles, are teacher favorites, and speak up more than boys. Also, not the whole population got surveyed, as the
    survey ignored homeschooled teens, who might have had different opinions than those in public or private
    schools, making the results biased.
    2. I wonder who the teenagers were who were surveyed? Were these teenagers all chosen from across the
    US or just in one section? I wonder if girls were more likely to say girls better represent all of the
    category instead of boys, and if so, if there were more girls surveyed? I wonder how many people chosen
    for the survey chose not to take it. I wonder what all of the responders' definition of each of the
    categories, for example, does better grades mean in one class or overall?
    3. This data reverses the normalized thought that boys are smarter than girls, better leaders, and more often
    teacher favorites. As a female, this data impacts me by showing me that around the US, girls are
    academically stronger and, on average, better leaders than males, which is motivating to try harder as a
    female to keep these trends going and to remove the negative stigma about female intelligence.
    4. In the US, teenagers say that females are more likely than males to excel in academic-related categories

raw_comment:
Click on the attached link and answer these 4 questions: 
    
    1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
    
    I noticed that for every category surveyed, both genders are about equal in the most common choice. Despite this, the second most populous selection was overwhelmingly girls in every category. 
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    
    I wonder why girls were so clearly the second choice, while the choice of boys was so rare in each category? Additionally, I wonder what the data would look like if the choice for both were removed, and if it would still favor girls. 
    
    3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
    
    This connects to me because I am a teenager aged 13 to 17 who still attends high school, so it is interesting to know how people perceive these categories based on gender. 
    
    4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
    
    "Who is better in school roles; Girls or Boys"

raw_comment:
1. I notice a strong perception that girls excel academically, with 55% of teenagers saying girls get better grades compared to only 42% who believe it is equal. I also notice that for most categories, the majority of teens see boys and girls as "about equal," but where an imbalance is perceived, it often favors girls. For instance, in "More leader roles," 27% see girls in more roles versus only 16% who see boys in more. The one area where a perceived imbalance favors boys is in being "Teacher favorites," where 16% see boys as favorites compared to only 6% for girls.
    
    2. I wonder why there is a perception that boys are more likely to be teacher's favorites despite girls being seen as getting better grades. I also wonder how these perceptions have changed over time and what specific actions or behaviors led to these results. Finally, I wonder if these perceptions influence the career choices and academic confidence of the teenagers themselves.
    
    3. This graph can impact a community by highlighting persistent gender stereotypes in schools. For students, believing that one gender is inherently better at academics or leadership could limit their own aspirations or create unfair expectations. For educators and parents, it serves as a call to examine their own biases and classroom practices to ensure they are fostering a truly equitable environment where all students feel they can excel and speak up.
    
    4. The Grade Gap: Teens See Girls Leading in School, But Boys as Teacher Favorites

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
    
    I notice that the most U.S. teenagers between 13-17 think that girls tend to excel more than boys in school related areas. 42% of teenagers say girls get better grades (compared to a much smaller percent for boys), and 34% say girls speak up more which is basically cut in half for boys.

    Would teachers and parents report similar perceptions? Why do so many teens see leadership as equal but not grades or speaking up?

    This graph highlights how gender perceptions influence school experiences. It might make students more aware of stereotypes about boys and girls in academics and leadership.
    
    4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
    
    "Who Excels at School? Teens Say It Depends on What You Measure"

Gender: it's there and (almost half the time) it matters
    
    On average, more than half the time gender appears to make no difference, which seems to make plenty of sense. Gender does not inherently change personality. A second observation is that of the gender differences noted (again a statistical minority of the subjects), there was a larger variance for girls. 
    
    I wonder if this is principally due to the various gender roles taught to girls in such a misogynistic society such as ours. Some girls are taught to stand by while others taught to stand up. Meanwhile, it has appeared that boys are generally taught without such extremes.
    
    To myself, it's a reminder that gender doesn't define anyone, but still can influence our experiences, particularly when we are children.
